timelines.title: Iran Nuclear Deal Negotiations and Regional Tensions

entries.update: Trump declared Abraham Accords participation 'mandatory' for any country seeking involvement in a prospective Iran deal. Trump publicly attacked critics of the emerging agreement, calling Democratic opponents, RINOs, and others 'weak and ineffective fools.' The Wall Street Journal editorial board warned the administration against offering Iran an 'economic bailout,' cautioning that ceasefire terms 'may deliver a strategic setback' for the U.S. Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid called the emerging framework 'a disaster.'

Fresh U.S. airstrikes on southern Iran on Monday cast doubt on the progress of ongoing negotiations, even as a fierce public relations battle over a potential deal continued. Trump's social media posts over the weekend created confusion regarding the status of the Iran negotiations, according to NBC News. Trump convened a Cabinet meeting Wednesday amid the ongoing negotiations and mounting criticism of the emerging deal. The EU launched a fertiliser plan in response to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz stemming from the Iran war, citing growing food security concerns in Europe.

President Trump called for more countries to recognize Israel as a condition for ending the war with Iran, proposing an expansion of the Abraham Accords. Analysts cited by the NY Times described the likelihood of such an expansion as close to zero, with the proposal being met with bewilderment across the Middle East.

President Trump made edits to a possible U.S.-Iran agreement, with requested changes related to the Strait of Hormuz and the removal of highly enriched uranium, according to CBS News and other U.S. media reports. French President Macron called on Middle Eastern leaders to help the U.S. and Iran seize a diplomatic opening, stating he met with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Omani Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, and Emirati leaders as part of these efforts. The United States proposed a 'roadmap' for de-escalation in Lebanon, according to a U.S. official. Israel's historic ground incursion into Lebanon is reported to be complicating ongoing Iran deal efforts. Trump's consideration of an Iran deal is sparking an intra-Republican debate, with Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker expected to lead opposition from defense hawks.

Iran suspended peace talks with the United States specifically to protest Israel's expanding offensive in Lebanon, with Iranian officials demanding a ceasefire on all fronts before negotiations could resume. President Trump told NBC News he had not been informed of the suspension.

Israel struck the southern suburbs of Beirut, with the Israeli military stating it targeted a Hezbollah command center or infrastructure. Trump publicly condemned the strikes on Truth Social and privately messaged Netanyahu to express disapproval, reportedly telling him he had 'no f***ing judgment,' according to Channel 12 and Axios reporter Barak Ravid. Despite Iran's earlier suspension of talks and the Israeli strikes, Defense Secretary Hegseth stated the U.S.-Iran deal remains 'on track,' and U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said the administration was 'confident' a final agreement would be signed Sunday. Trump declared the deal imminent and had previously stated it could be signed on his 80th birthday Sunday, though Iran's state-run Fars News Agency disputed this timeline, stating Tehran had 'neither finalized nor officially declared its position.' According to Tehran, the framework includes Iran agreeing not to build a nuclear weapon and to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for approximately $25 billion in frozen assets being released. Congressional reaction was mixed, with Sen. Lankford calling for ratification, Sen. Reed calling it a costly 'birthday gift,' and former Obama Deputy Secretary of State Wendy Sherman describing the deal's proposed 60-day timeframe as 'pretty short.' The U.S.-Iran war is expected to dominate Trump's upcoming G7 trip to France, overshadowing the summit's originally planned agenda.

Lebanon and the Israel-Hezbollah conflict have emerged as a primary obstacle to the broader U.S.-Iran deal, having shifted from a secondary front to a central sticking point, according to the New York Times. The Iran deal's oil sanctions waivers drew criticism from Iran hawks, including some Trump allies, who argued the move surrenders key economic leverage over Tehran.
